rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage contrasts the fate of Qur’an rejecters with that of people who denied the hereafter, whose loss becomes clear when the Hour suddenly arrives.
rows.anchor: these verses depict the fate of the rejecters of the hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section extends reassurance to Muhammad and his companions; its rebuke and anger are directed at stubborn rejecters demanding a miracle.
rows.anchor: This section dwells further on this topic of assurance. In fact, there occurs an emphatic enhancement in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad’s affection made him wish for a miracle that might lead his people to faith, but God assures him that they deny God’s revelations rather than him.
rows.anchor: These people are not denying him; they are actually denying God’s revelations.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier prophets also faced rejection and endured it patiently, so Muhammad should do likewise in keeping with God’s established practice.
rows.anchor: Prophets who came before him were similarly rejected; they bore this rejection with patience and hence he too should do the same.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God could force people to believe instantly, but the passage says he has not chosen to do so.
rows.anchor: if God wanted to forcibly make people accept faith, this would have happened in the blink of an eye.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reference to Abraham and later prophets asserts that they invited people to Muhammad’s same message; Muhammad must follow their guidance and leave rejecters to themselves, since he must preach but cannot force belief.
rows.anchor: His responsibility is to only preach and he is not liable to force people to accept guidance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham is singled out because Israelites and Ishmaelites both claimed him as patriarch and guide while attributing their inherited religious practices to him.
rows.anchor: both the Israelites and the Ishmaelites regarded him as their patriarch and spiritual leader.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Judaism, Christianity, and Ishmaelite polytheism are later fabrications with no connection to Abraham; Muhammad’s mission revives and completes Abraham’s religion for his descendants.
rows.anchor: it was also essential to make it evident to the Ishmaelites that the religion of polytheism they have adopted is their own fabrication

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s naming of Abraham’s father as Āzar resolves variant pronunciations in Jewish scripture; as guardian of earlier scriptures and direct revelation, its pronunciation is authoritative.
rows.anchor: The way the Qur’ ān has specifically mentioned his name shows that it wants to resolve this difference of opinion in its pronunciation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jewish religious literature says Āzar worshipped, made, and sold idols; Islahi suggests he may have been his temple’s chief priest.
rows.anchor: Āzar not only worshipped idols, he also manufactured and sold them. It may well be that he be the chief priest of his temple.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s birth to an idolatrous father and his campaign against the father’s beliefs and profession manifest God’s power; prophets first convey truth to those closest to them.
rows.anchor: Amongst the signs of the veracity of prophets of God is the sign that the truth they invite people to is foremost conveyed by them to those closest and dearest to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage briefly summarizes Abraham’s address to his father and points to fuller treatments elsewhere.
rows.anchor: The message towards which Abraham (sws) invited his father is only briefly referred to here. At other instances, it is detailed out as well:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s question about making idols deities exposes his people’s obvious deviation and echoes his challenge to worship things they carved themselves.
rows.anchor: The words “have you made idols as your deities?” of Abraham (sws) are meant to point at the blatantly evident deviance of his people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “in this way We show,” an incomplete verb meaning “We were showing” is understood as omitted, following a common Arabic construction.
rows.anchor: According to a common Arabic style, an incomplete verb is suppressed here.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Malakūt is derived on the pattern of rahabūt, literally conveys authority or kingdom, and in Qur’anic usage denotes God’s dominion over all creation.
rows.anchor: literally means “respect, authority and kingdom.” However, in the Qur’ān it refers to God’s kingdom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an repeatedly calls people to contemplate God’s kingdom, as illustrated by its references to the heavens and earth and to God’s control of all things.
rows.anchor: It has repeatedly invited people to reflect on this kingdom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reflecting on the heavens and earth leads to sound concepts and deeds and helps answer questions about creation, the Creator, life’s purpose, truth, accountability, and divine governance.
rows.anchor: by reflecting on this system one is led to true concepts and deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A scientist may study the universe for immediate practical gain while overlooking the Creator’s wisdom and providence, visible even in a flower’s beauty.
rows.anchor: he does this by making his own self or his limited environment as its focal point. He is only keen to see his immediate benefit.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Newton’s discovery of gravity opened useful scientific laws, yet insight should ask who bound all things by attraction; the honest answer is a wise, powerful Creator.
rows.anchor: who is it that has bound every single object, big or small in this law of mutual attraction?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People who honestly contemplate the universe and accept its implications receive a share of prophetic insight according to their ability; the verse describes Abraham’s special, divinely granted vision.
rows.anchor: Other individuals too gain its share in accordance with their ability. These individuals are ones who honestly reflect on this universe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted coordinated clause in the verse is recovered from context: God showed Abraham the kingdom so he could convince his people and attain full conviction.
rows.anchor: if the suppressed part is revealed, the whole sense would be: “and, in this way, We would make Abraham observe the kingdom of the heavens and the earth  so that he may conclusively convey the truth to his people and become among those who have full conviction.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Full conviction exceeds ordinary belief, comes through reflection and observation rather than intuition, and has no ceiling; prophets possess it and devoted followers share it.
rows.anchor: conviction is acquired by reflection and deliberation and by observing and having knowledge of God’s kingdom. There is no upper limit to this conviction.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of Abraham’s observation of the star, moon, and sun expands the earlier brief statement: their submission to divine laws shows that only their Creator deserves worship.
rows.anchor: they explain the brevity found in the previous verses. Previously, it was stated how Abraham (sws) exposed the hollow nature of the religion followed by his father and his nation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets share a preaching purpose but adjust style to their audience and temperament; John and Jesus use parables, while other prophets may sermonize or use legal diction.
rows.anchor: owing to the peculiar temperament and nature of their addressees, every prophet has some distinctive features with regard to his style of preaching and methodology of reasoning.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s argumentative audience often refused to listen and quickly turned to polemics, so he used gradual reasoning to lead them into a position where they had no answer.
rows.anchor: Abraham’s nation was very inclined to polemical debates and argumentation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idol-smashing episode exemplifies Abraham’s method: he directed people to ask the surviving idol and its victims, eliciting their admission that idols cannot speak or defend themselves.
rows.anchor: He also gestured towards the shattered idols and asked them to inquire from these victims because if they speak, they will narrate what calamity befell them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham also used turiya: a true statement that can mislead listeners until his plan has unfolded; Islahi postpones its fuller example and lexical discussion to al-Saffat.
rows.anchor: As per this device, in order to carry out his plan, he would give a statement that would be true but could potentially mislead his addressees.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gradual reasoning and turiya may be punctuated with polite humor; light humor is also a prophetic trait, with examples to come in al-Anbiya and al-Saffat.
rows.anchor: light and polite humour is also a trait of prophets of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham may have seen Venus or another star and said “This is my Lord” aloud as self-talk that listeners could hear, allowing him to raise doubt without directly provoking them.
rows.anchor: It is possible that this be Venus or could be some other. He said that this was his Lord.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The star episode draws attention to both rising and setting: regular disappearance shows the heavenly bodies are governed, and the audience was prompted to question their inherited belief.
rows.anchor: When they set after rising and go after coming and that too with such punctuality that there is not the slightest change in their direction, time and shape, then they by their very existence they show that they are being governed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham presents the Creator’s relation with worshippers as love rather than mere fear; fading heavenly objects are themselves subservient and cannot merit that love.
rows.anchor: a person’s relationship with his creator and master is that of love and not mere fear.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The moon scene advances the lesson: worshipping things that fade is serious error, a cause for sorrow, and people depend on God alone for guidance.
rows.anchor: What becomes further evident is that this error is not small. It is a matter of great sorrow and yearning.

rows.speaker: some exegetes
rows.claim: Some exegetes take Abraham’s conditional statement about guidance as referring to the past; Islahi says this reading needlessly stretches the text.
rows.anchor: Some exegetes opine that this condition relates to the past

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s words about needing guidance state a general truth and do not mean he was previously astray; he holds up his noble nature as a mirror to his people.
rows.anchor: Saying these words does not necessitate that Abraham (sws) was in error earlier or thought that he was in error.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the sun “the greatest” is sarcastic; after it sets, Abraham publicly disavows the deities, having earlier spoken indirectly through self-address.
rows.anchor: This time, however, he added the words “it is the greatest.” It is very evident that he said these words in a sarcastic way to mock at them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s final declaration expressly turns away from the people’s partners and devotes him to the Creator of the heavens and earth, expressing monotheism and submission.
rows.anchor: These words depict monotheism and submission in a grand way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction of “I have turned my face” also carries the sense of devotion or submission, which is why the prayer begins with these words.
rows.anchor: Since in the prayer we acknowledge this reality, it begins with an utterance of these words.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Abraham’s disavowal, his people threaten him with their deities’ wrath; Islahi explains that this fear reflects polytheism’s foundation.
rows.anchor: Since polytheism is based on fear, they began to threaten and warn him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s people did not deny God but associated partners with him; Islahi generalizes that nations err through corrupting monotheism rather than denying God.
rows.anchor: his people never denied God; they only associated partners with him. And this is not something specific to his people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham says the supposed deities cannot harm him unless God wills, displaying trust in God; Shu‘ayb’s parallel shows even sincere aims require divine help through trials.
rows.anchor: These words showed his tremendous trust in God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Abraham’s people ascribe partners to God without proof, they rather than he should fear; the question of which faction merits security exposes their culpability.
rows.anchor: it is they who have associated partners with him without any proof.
